quote: Sinn der Kugel Cylinder etc. Funktionen, zur Annäherung an die häufigst vorkommenden Körperformen.
english: Meaning of the sphere, cylinder, etc. functions, for approximating the most frequently occurring body shapes.
topic: Notes on simultaneously approximating the integrals of a second-order linear differential equation (analogous to the Jacobi continued fraction algorithm) to draw conclusions about transcendence, on treating a free fluid jet with cylinder functions, and on Kronecker's attitude toward the logical foundations of mathematics.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a precise research problem. It's a conceptual or methodological remark about why the special functions of mathematical physics exist and what they mean. Spherical harmonics and Legendre functions, cylinder (Bessel) functions, and others like Lamé, Mathieu and spheroidal functions come from separating variables in the Laplace or Helmholtz equation in coordinate systems whose coordinate surfaces fit the most common body shapes (sphere, cylinder, ellipsoid and so on). This makes boundary-value problems on those bodies solvable by series expansions. In modern terms the question is: which orthogonal coordinate systems allow separation of variables for Δu=0 or Δu+k²u=0, and which special functions arise from each?
triage.answered_by: The theory was already being systematized around Hilbert's time. Maxime Bôcher's 'Über die Reihenentwickelungen der Potentialtheorie' (Teubner, Leipzig, 1894) treated the special functions of potential theory as products of separation in confocal cyclidic coordinates. L. P. Eisenhart (Phys. Rev. 45, 427, 1934) later classified the 11 coordinate systems in which the Helmholtz equation separates. Laplace's equation also separates, in the partial R-separable sense, in further systems such as bispherical and toroidal coordinates. Work in the 1970s, presented at the Springer conference 'Symmetries of differential equations in mathematical physics', linked separable systems to symmetry groups. No one is recorded as answering Hilbert's note specifically.

evidence.claim: Bôcher's 1894 monograph 'Die Reihenentwickelungen der Potentialtheorie' (Teubner, Leipzig) is the classic reference for separation of variables in potential theory and is still cited in modern separation-of-variables papers.
Eisenhart (Phys. Rev. 45, 427, 1934) showed that there are eleven coordinate systems in which the equation is separable.
Laplace's equation can be solved by separation of variables in the 11 coordinate systems, and two more (bispherical and toroidal) bring the total to 13.
Laplace's equation can be solved by separation of variables in all 11 coordinate systems in which the Helmholtz equation separates (MathWorld).
Separation of variables in less common (asymmetric cyclidic) coordinate systems is still being worked out, which continues the Bôcher line of work.
A Springer conference chapter studies differential equations of mathematical physics from the point of view of symmetry groups and separation of variables.

triage.why: The note reads as Hilbert reflecting on what spherical and cylinder functions are for: they come from separating variables in coordinates adapted to common body shapes. That's a heuristic or teaching point, not a well-posed open problem. It isn't among the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The explanation behind it was standard by the 1890s (Bôcher 1894) and was later made into a classification (Eisenhart 1934, then the symmetry-group approach to separation of variables). Some separation-of-variables work in unusual coordinates continues, but none of it addresses Hilbert's remark, so I can't call this an active research question. My searches found no source that discusses this diary entry, so linking it to Bôcher and Eisenhart is my reading of the context, not something a source documents.
